blocks.label: Course recap and overview of learning outcomes
blocks.content: [background chatter] All righty. Shall we get going? I hope you guys have been having fun in the practicals. Has it been very evident, the story that the cancer can tell you in the tissues? Hopefully, we will get some insight and try and apply what we saw in the histopathology practicals in cancer and try now to decide what's going on in individual cells. So hopefully, in the practicals, you appreciated some of the cellular changes that you can see from the normal cells and what happens when they transform in terms of their shape, with the pleomorphism, the hetero-- What is it? The increase in color, in staining, and some of the other transformed properties that they have. We're going to go through each of those and the kind of genetic changes today, and what can lead to some of the transformation. But I think in order for us to do that, we're going to start with a little bit of history because sometimes it's easier to understand where we are now in terms of our knowledge with how we got there. So I have a new pointer today. Just to go through our learning outcomes for today, so we're going to see how cellular transformation, what it looks like, how we thought it was caused by viruses, and this conception that has led from the study of tumor viruses to this idea of oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes. We're going to look at what transformation does, and we're going to contrast the activities of oncogenes and tumor suppressive genes and the other categories that cancer biologists use in terms of things like gatekeepers and caretakers, and also driver and passenger mutations, initiation and maintenance of tumors, things like this. And we're going to talk about genetic instability and what this is as a feature of cancer and how this speeds up and changes the dynamics and the rate of tumor development, and we will talk about hereditary predispositions to cancers. Okay. So hopefully by the end of the lecture, you should have a grasp on all of those things.

blocks.label: Early cell theory and germ theory of disease
blocks.content: Starting with cell and germ theories really, our modern concepts of cells being the building blocks of life arise out of, if you like, a technological advancement in microscopes. Right? You hopefully will be familiar with Robert Hooke's Micrographia one of the books that's actually quite easy to see in Cambridge because there are multiple copies of it floating around in various college libraries. And this picture is quite famous. He's actually not looking at individual cells here but this idea of, in the cork bark, this idea of sub-cellular structure or cellular structure to tissues. The Dutch scientist Van Leeuwenhoek used microscopes to find smaller and smaller microorganisms. But you'll see that between the development of the technology in the 1600s all the way to the 1800s, couple hundred years later, it took before there was the proposition that plants and animals are made of cells, this kind of cellular theory of life. With the advent of microorganisms being discovered, Mycobacterium being one of them in 1882, around the late '80s and the early 1990s there were many very famous scientists whose names you will recognize that contributed to the germ theory of disease, that each of the diseases that we have is caused by microorganisms; things like anthrax, rabies, dysentery, cholera. And also the advent of vaccination which is, of course, one of the major public health interventions that's resulted in improvements in human health. It wasn't such a leap to think that cancer was the result of an infection and is a transmissible disease.

blocks.content: This idea that cancer is a transmissible disease kind of took hold and so with the advent of Rous sarco virus people went looking for more transforming viruses and this was pretty much the assay that they were trying to use in the .40s and the '50s looking for these transforming viruses They found a whole bunch of them.Right?There are many DNA and RNA viruses that can transform cells and cause tumors to grow I’ve put a list of them here You can see that they cause tumors humans also in other animalsYou’ll see that there are different ones uhthat umin different families as wellUhand sothere's no real rhymeor reason tothe typeofvirus thatcanendupbeingatransforming virus But actually, overall when they were discovering these viruses, they kind of noticed that the epidemiology didn't really fit. For the vast majority of cancers that are there, there really isn't a viral etiology for them. Worldwide, the burden of cancer that's caused by infectious viruses is around 25% of the cases. So it is actually a large burden on human populations, but it's actually very few viruses altogether, and most of them are listed here. And Professor Turner will have told you about many of them as well. So things like hepatitis B and C as well, here both DNA and RNA viruses. Many herpesviruses, human herpesvirus 8 KSHV EBV, these also cause tumors in human populations or associated with them. And things like retrovirus HTLV-1 which causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. So there's quite a few. There's only really seven. There's a new one that's not on this list which is Merkel cell polyomavirus, which is also a rare tumor that's associated with a viral infection.

blocks.label: Retroviral provirus integration and proto-oncogene capture
blocks.content: But this principle of that there are some viruses that do cause cancers was very important-- oh I got two now -- to understand the idea of transforming genes. Right? You have to kind of understand a little bit of a retrovirus' life cycle to understand what genes would be acquired that would give that formerly just if you like a benign retrovirus turn it into a transforming virus. And that's because retroviruses when they infect, they use reverse transcriptase to turn their genomes into DNA proviruses, which actually insert into the genome. And they do this randomly so they can insert almost anywhere in the genome. They jump around and it's often based on things like chromatin accessibility and transcription, things like this. So you can get integration of this provirus just about anywhere in the genome. Here you just have going about its business cellular SRC locus. Here comes this provirus and it inserts in front of it and what you would get is coexpression of the provirus because there'll be a very strong promoter for the virus to express its genes and you'll also get then transcription through the cellular SRC gene. And over time there might be a mutation that's acquired or there might be some drift here and you'll get versions of this cellular protooncogene known as vSRC or viral SRC. Then this gets packaged into a capsid and piggybacks along with the viral genome and now becomes a transforming retrovirus. So started off just as a regular old retrovirus and end up being a transforming retrovirus here.

blocks.label: Testing oncogenic mutations in immortalized cell models
blocks.content: And then you can also take your gene out of your cancer of interest and look for the effect of specific mutations on that gene, because very often genes will be mutated in cancer. And again, there's the idea of taking your gene from your tumor cell, transfecting it into cells. Here you're combining it with lipid particles, putting them onto cells. You'll get a focus formation. That cell you may test in a mouse to see whether or not you get a tumor. And again, this is what this looks like. So this was a very classic test that still takes place using NIH. These are mouse embryonic fibroblasts that have been transformed usually through one of two mutations, not important which ones. But when you add something like a mutated Ras from a cancer, you'll see that you get that focus formation. The morphology of the cells is very changed, and they will end up forming a tumor on a mouse. And so in this way you can test some of the cancer mutations that you're studying, the point mutations, the translocations, and you can do this using a Lox/Cre system, amplifications, deletions using CRISPR, and use a virus to insert across the genome causing either activation or inactivation of your gene, and also using genetic models. So there's a whole host of tests that one can do in the lab to do this. And you'll remember that we're just using individual cells here. NI3T3 cells are not cancer cells, they're just immortalized cells. So we're looking to see a change not just in the lifespan of the cell but a change in its properties and its functionality, and it will have all of those things that we listed on the other slide. So lots of different ways that you can test this.

blocks.label: Classification of oncogenes, tumor suppressors, drivers, and caretakers
blocks.content: Okay. So [lip smacks] in doing so, you're going to say whether or not the activity of that gene or that mutation is either if you like promoting tumor growth or hindering it. And so it kind of leads to this classification which I'm sure you're familiar with, but actually when you're a cancer biologist, it's a little bit limiting in a way. It's a very good definition but it also kind of arises out of this tumor virology field, right? So the definitions of this can vary quite a bit, but one that we use and one that is a useful tool is that an oncogenic mutation is a mutation that results in increased activity of the normal gene, and this is always relative to wild type. So whenever we're talking about the activities, we're talking about what it does compared to the wild type, to the normal gene. So there's an increase in activity, and this also has to help the tumor to form. okay? So as a result, it's usually, not always, a dominant mutation, and usually you only have to have one copy of the gene mutated. Right? You can contrast that with a tumor-suppressive mutation. These mutations will result in a loss of the function of the gene and the activity-- the function of the gene is to restrain tumor formation. As it is a loss of function this is usually a recessive mutation and usually both copies of the gene have to be mutated in order for that recessive activity or that function to be lost. Okay. It's pretty straightforward, but it's not the only way in which cancer biologists talk about the activity of a mutation. We also talk about drivers, and these would be mutations that actually are directly involved in tumorigenesis. As you will come to appreciate that cancer genomes can be heavily mutate,d and it's very hard to figure out which mutation is actually important in driving the tumor. So they talk about driver mutations and passenger mutations, and these mutations might have activities in terms of promoting or preventing tumor formation at different times in tumor development. So there are drivers, passengers, and they're also thinking about the functions of these genes; gatekeeper mutations which are involved in restraining cell cycle or proliferation and growth, and also caretakers which are involved in whole cellular integrity and maintenance of the genome.Okay? So lots of different ways in which we can describe it and they're pretty interchangeable in that some people prefer some definitions over others.

blocks.label: Rb phosphorylation and regulation of the G1/S checkpoint
blocks.content: Okay? So this should be basic revision for you in terms of the cell cycle. Cells are in a quiescent phase. Most of our cells are terminally differentiated except for our highly proliferative tissues like our blood, our skin, our gut which is turning over quite heavily. In order to do that they enter this growth preparation phase in G1, DNA replication in S phase, the checking phase in G2 getting ready for mitosis and mitosis.Right? So one of the key control points -- I have to hold both of these – is the G1 to S checkpoint here which is regulated by the retinoblastoma protein, uh, and this is pretty much a very hard stop unless all of the right signals are received in order to proceed through the cell cycle. This is a large protein. It runs at over 105 kilodaltons on a gel, and it has a lot of phosphoacceptocytes, about 14 of them that are scattered through, but a lot of them at the C terminus that can be phosphorylated by cyclin dependent kinases which are of course the kinases that drive progression through the cell cycle.In this early part of the cell cycle the starter kinase or the one that really receives all the signals from the extracellular and also the intracellular environment that assembles in response to mitogen and growth signals are the D-type cyclins of which there are three, and the CDK four and six kinases which can bind to any of those three kinases. So they have the capacity to phosphorylate Rb, and in doing so will inactivate RB and so release this block on cell cycle progression.okay? So

blocks.label: CDK inhibitors and oncogenic disruption of G1/S control
blocks.content: in addition to this regulatory step there's additional regulators that act on top of it There are a family of INK which are inhibitor of kinases of which there are four of these, but p16 is the one that is the most famous if you like, and it prevents the activator from binding to the kinase So it prevents this complex from forming, and you also have p21 of which there are three of these that can bind this ternary complex straddling it like a cowboy on a saddle and preventing this activity from phosphorylating Rb. So there's lots of different levels of regulation that can occur here. So in terms of thinking about this as oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes, you can think about it like this. So tumor suppressor genes would be mutations, either deletions or silencing or methylation or binding by viral oncoproteins that can inactivate their activity. So any of these mutations in these genes that would either prevent the activity of inhibitor or relieve repression, these are always double negatives in terms of thinking of how they work. So these would be tumor suppressive mutations, and any oncogenic mutations that you would get would result in an increase in the activity here that would have more kinase activity that would inactivate RB. So some of the oncogenic mutations that you can see in this pathway include things like amplification of the D-type cyclins or other activating mutations of CDK4/6. You can also get viral insertion in the promoters to increase the expression of the D-type cyclins. So the net effect on this pathway is to relieve repression of the G1 to S checkpoint. And so-- Whoops, let me go back. So what that means is that this pathway is compromised and so you get continual if you like passage through the cell cycle here. This is much less well regulated and so you can get premature entry into S phase by the cell.

blocks.label: Dominant vs recessive mutation phenotypes in cancer genes
blocks.content: What does that look like in terms of mutations? It kind of looks like this. As I said normally you have two wild type copies of your gene In terms of a cancer cell gaining a mutation, you'd have one mutation -this would be a dominant mutation -you'd have an increase in activity of something that promotes tumor growth, and so this would be a dominant mutation. A classic tumor suppressor gene like RB again you start with two wild type copies; you get a mutation but because you still have a wild type copy of the gene here , you could have no effect because you have enough of this protein to complement the lack of that protein and so you need to actually have two mutations lose this activity, to inactivate this activity before you get an abnormal phenotype of the cell. Right. There are other versions of these kinds of mutations and you get some tumor suppressive genes things like P53 where you have two wild top copies and if you gain one um mutation uh in the gene actually that's enough for the cell to register as a slightly abnormal or somewhat abnormal phenotype. Uh and you can go on to lose two copies but already with just one mutation you already have an abnormal phenotype [background sneeze]. So this gets to the crux of why these definitions are a little bit less than perfect. And that's because you have to really consider the type of mutation that you're getting and the effect on the function in the cell, and then also the effect on the tumor right. So you almost need to consider each mutation separately in order to understand what it's doing.

blocks.label: Dominant-negative mechanics of p53 tetrameric disruption
blocks.content: All right. What does that mean? I'll give you one example in P53 since it's on the other slide.You have to understand that P53 is transcription factor and it binds DNA as tetramer (a multimeric complex). So you need four good copies of the gene or the protein rather in order for it to be fully functional and to work in best optimal way. Here if you get a mutation in P53 the wild type allele is still making these lovely blue copies which are wild type and functional and you have mutant copy and in this case the mutation is in the DNA binding domain of P53 and its producing a protein. Because it's tetrameric you get all these potential combinations of wild type P53 multimering with a mutant version of the P53 protein that can't really bind the DNA particularly well. You will see that 15/16ths of the potential combination of them are comprised in terms of their DNA binding capacity. You only have one tetramer here that has four good wild type copies of P53 and the rest of them all have a mutant in there which means that it's not going to able to bind DNA as well.It will be somewhat abnormal, somewhat have lost P53 mutation.A good way for you visualize what this looks like is to look at the effect of point mutation in mouse model.Here we have two wild type alleles of P53 in stem cell and engineer in a point mutation.In one case you can engineer null mutation .Just make truncating mutation at very start left with one wild type copy and in this case a null copy.What would you get loads and loads of blue good wild type copies of P53 and the only thing that you would get there is the multimetric wild type copies.Actually with wild type allele and null allele you have what looks phenotypically normal cell That mutation doesn’t make difference However If you make a wild type copy with a point mutation that affects the DNA binding domain end up with this effect.This version of P53 with point mutation acts as dominant negative takes out most of the P53 function and it's almost dead for P53 The affect of the mutation on the protein makes big difference Then off course on the cells interms of tumour promotion

blocks.label: Distinguishing sequence instability from chromosomal instability
blocks.content: Right. So we're going to move on to this idea now of genetic instability. We have our little map, as we said. Cancer results from a stepwise accumulation of mutations that moves the cell from a normal to slightly abnormal to malignant state over time. And what we don't know is the number of mutations that this requires and how quickly this goes, and if they're always the same in all the different tissues. So now let's consider what would happen if the tumor became genetically unstable. So what exactly does that look like? Well, there are different types of genetic instability, right? And one of the important things to take away here is that genetic instability is an abnormality of cancer cells. It's not because the cells are growing faster. It is a specific defect that they have. It's not because they're forgetting to grow and they're just growing. That's not it. It is an abnormality that they have. So just to show you what this looks like, I'm giving you here two karyotype spreads or chromosome metaphase spreads of two different cancer cell lines that are used very frequently in the lab. These are both colorectal cancer cell lines, and these are karyotypes, metaphase spreads of the chromosomes in those cells. And in each case, they're painted with a different color dye so that you can see the chromosomes and pair them up. And when they do these, they order them from biggest to smallest, and they number them in this way. So what you can see for Tumor A is that it's pretty much a diploid cancer. Right? A diploid cell. You have two of each of the copies. There is a little bit of noise. You do have some slight little bits of different colored chromosomes that are present on the wrong chromosome, so to speak. But for the most part, this is a diploid cancer. And you can contrast that with Tumor B here, where you have multiple different numbers of chromosomes. So here you have four, here you have three, here you have four. And you can see that these chromosomes are also rainbow-colored in terms of the numbers of breaks. You have a lot of different fusions and translocations that are going on in this tumor. So we would call this phenotype a chromosome instability because it doesn't have a diploid karyotype. Right? It has an aneuploid polyploidy karyotype here. However, if you were to sequence this tumor, and by that I mean things like Illumina sequencing, where you're using short sequences to look at the DNA sequence of each of the individual genes that's present within this tumor, you'd see that the sequence is actually stable. Yes, there are a lot of translocations. But the sequence-- They are not point mutations, or any of these small deletions or inversions. But what you do find is that if you sequenced this tumor, you'd find a lot of sequence instability here. Lots of point mutations. In fact, 100 times higher level of sequence mutations in this tumor. Lots of point mutations, insertions, deletions, and things like that. Small sequence mutations. Right? So two different types of genetic instability that we're looking at here.

blocks.label: DNA repair origins and faithful excision repair pathways
blocks.content: So it has big implications for us thinking about how does this genetic instability come about? Because now you're getting to the crux of why the tumor started in the first place. Right? So there are a lot of different ways in which this can arise owing to a failure to repair DNA damage in terms of the normal metabolism of DNA, and also just mistakes made during replication and mitosis. Obviously, we have a very high demand to have, as we said, during the cell cycle sequence fidelity and chromosome fidelity in maintaining genome integrity with every different cell cycle. And so there's a very high demand to replicate faithfully the ten to the thirteenth different base pairs that you have in your genome. So this is supposed to be error free kind of method of doing it. But obviously, this comes about with a lot of different levels of regulation and checks on this process. And so a failure to repair or making mistakes and then failing to repair will result in sequence instability and chromosome instability. As I said, when we talk about sequence instability, we're talking about small scale insertions, deletions, point mutations, and chromosome instability are much larger bigger rearrangements and translocations, and almost uses a different type of assay to detect as opposed to just sequencing. Okay. So we're just going to run through the main types of DNA damage and repair and what these pathways look like. So I'm just gonna talk briefly about nucleotide excision repair and base excision repair because they really aren't big players in cancer. And the reason for that is that they, as you can see here well, you can't really see it, I'll just tell you. Things like intrastrand dimers that form or damage to individual bases. This is quite easy for the cell to fix. It will have sensors that will, for example, detect an aberration here in the helix here. It'll come out as a loop, and it will detect that, and it will come and cut out if you like, the damaged base or the thymine dimer that's present, and it will copy the sequence off the other strand. Right? So it's very faithful repair, and as long as these pathways are intact, you can get a good copy made. Similarly, a single-strand break here on the backbone of the DNA, it's very easy to fix. There's no threat to the integrity of the sequence. And so it really is something that can be easily fixed by the cell without any loss of DNA sequence.

blocks.label: Mismatch repair failure, replication slippage, and microsatellite instability
blocks.content: Where the trouble comes in is when you have things like here, which is a mismatch in the cell where you have inappropriate pairing of the bases So this T to G pairing obviously shouldn't be there. And if the cell doesn't sense this and fix it, and you go through another round of replication, obviously you'll end up with a change in the base pair sequence. So this would be a problem. And this also includes something known as replication slippage. Replication slippage occurs when you have multiple repeats one after the other, and what happens is that when the cell is aligning the DNA to replicate it, it actually aligns-- It does pair correctly, but because there are a lot of repeats sometimes it excludes some of the pairs. So the pairing happens correctly, but you can result in extra expansion of these repeat sequences. Repeat sequences are really hard for polymerases to make sure that they're copying them correctly. Right? So when you have mutations in mismatch repair genes, you get these kinds of problems, which is that you get incorrect pairing and then copying that mistake through to the next generation of the cell. And you also get replication slippages of repeat sequences, which causes them to expand and shrink over time. So this was something that when cancer biologists were looking for markers in the genomes, they noticed that these, what they call microsatellites of DNA, were unstable in their size. So they used to expand and contract and expand and contract, and this became the hallmark for understanding that that cancer cell has a mutation in one of the mismatched repair enzymes that recognizes and helps to repair these kind of inappropriate base pairs. This seems to be something that is very prevalent in colorectal cancer. Okay? So that is one of these defects, and that is what it looks like here. As I said, there's sequence instability here, and this cell line has a mutation in the mismatch repair pathway.

blocks.label: Double-strand break repair: Homologous recombination vs error-prone joining
blocks.content: Obviously, that's not going to be the case for tumor B. For tumor B, we have a problem with the double-strand break repair pathway. Now, these are very dangerous for the cell. Right? So by the time you have a double-strand break, the possibility for that piece of broken DNA to float away from where it's supposed to be and not be correctly repaired. So obviously, there are two important pathways. Hopefully, you've come across homologous recombination and nonhomologous end joining. The homologous recombination pathway is the safe pathway, but can really only operate during S and G2 phase. So there are a number of proteins that are involved in this. Actually, a large number of proteins that are involved in this. And the ones that you might be familiar with are BRCA1 and BRCA2. These are important proteins that help with homologous recombination. And just to take you through how that works, when there is a double strand break, there are exonucleases that will come and chew back and reveal single stranded ends. These single stranded ends are very quickly recognized by the cell. They're single strand binding proteins that help to stabilize them and allow them to do something called strand invasion. So the strand invasion happens with the sister chromatid. As I said, the undamaged copy has to serve as the template for this repair. So this can only happen after the cell has actually replicated its genome. So you have this sister chromatid, and you get strand invasion, and then you can get extension and copying from that intact allele. And then there's extension again from the three prime, and you get this holiday junction, as it's known, that allows this copying to take place. And then this is resolved, and then you get ligation of these free ends here and here, and then you get a damage-free restored sequence, lovely copy of your double-stranded break mended by homologous recombination. So this is very high fidelity and really the preferred method [coughing] of repair and can happen, as I said, in late S and G2 phase. This is really what G2 phase is for. It's for checking for the fidelity and the repair of any damage that you have in your replicated genome. But what happens if you have a double-stranded break, not during S and G2 phase, any other part of the cell cycle? Or alternatively, if you have a mutation in the proteins that metabolize homologous recombination. So you get this double-strand break, and as I said, you get this resectioning, but there's no sister chromatid available now. So now you have these single stranded bits of DNA that are wafting about and have nothing to pair with. And so what they will do generally is try and find regions of micro homology within themselves. Right? And so you'll get a little bit of limited base pairing that occurs, and then they will just extend from whatever they can find. Right? So they basically just stick two things together. You'll get a filling in reaction, a ligation, and you'll get small deletions, small insertions, and small mutations that occur. But most importantly, what you get now is a loss of sequence fidelity. So this is very error prone and not really the way you want to repair your genome. right? This is the bad way to do it. Right? So that is actually what's happening in this tumor, tumor B, because it has mutations in the BRCA2 gene, and that's the gene that's involved in homologous recombination. So you have a lot of these just sticking of chromosomes together where they can. And so that's why this looks so messy in terms of the number of chromosomes and actually the constituent parts of the chromosomes that are all just stuck together. Right? So this is what chromosomal instability looks like Okay.

blocks.label: DNA polymerase epsilon proofreading mutations
blocks.content: So I've told you now this failure or mutations in the DNA repair machinery in a cancer cell can lead to sequence instability or to chromosomal instability, and now we're going to cover things like errors in DNA replication or in mitosis. And one of the examples of this is if the cancer cell was to acquire a mutation in DNA polymerase epsilon. So the polymerase epsilon is really one of the core machinery to replicate your DNA during S phase. It also has a very strong proofreading function associated with it to make sure that there's fidelity in what's actually being copied. And so tumors that have mutations in polymerase epsilon are amongst the most mutated cancers that there are. Right? So they have huge numbers of point mutations. And so it is possible just to gain a mutation like that and which will render you sequence unstable.

blocks.label: Mitotic chromosome segregation defects and cellular stress cascades
blocks.content: So in terms of chromosomal instability, I have a few movies to show you, which I will just start on away because they actually take a bit of time. Whoops. Has it started? No. Maybe I just have to do this. Yes, that's it. I know these are fuzzy. You can always go onto these websites and do it. This is what happens when you blow them up. So everybody loves mitosis. It's always good to see. You can see it in the tissues. Somebody was asking me in the demonstration about how can you spot mitoses and these hypermitotic cells. You can always spot the fuzzy condensed chromosomes, metaphase, anaphase, and that's kind of what that looks like. It's very normal. If you end up with a tumor with chromosomal instability, you get a very different looking thing. And you can see that the chromosomes fail to come to the metaphase plate, and they lag, and they stay outside of the metaphase plate. And this activates the spindle assembly checkpoint because not all of the chromosomes are aligned. And so mitosis will be halted until all of the material gets to the metaphase plate. So we wait, and then it's there, and then as soon as that-- Then you go through mitosis or the cell will go through mitosis. All right? So this is what it looks like. And it went very quickly that you couldn't see the lagging chromosome, which you can see here. There's still a bit there and there it is there. And these lagging chromosomes are important to understand why this would be a problem. And this is again what this looks like here, and this is because the spindle fibers are attached on both sides. So you end up with these lagging chromosomes. So defects in the way that the cell undertakes mitosis can also lead to problems for the cell. And so these lagging chromosomes have a big effect [coughing] on the cell. And just to say that in addition to this, there's also epigenetic instability although I won't cover much more on that. But I have added this because people were asking me what does it mean if you just have this chromosome hanging out outside that doesn't segregate at the right time. Well, it can have big consequences for the cancer cell. It can end up outside of the nucleus altogether in a micronucleus, for example. You have this kind of extra chromosomal DNA that ends up outside in a micronucleus, right? So it has big consequences. There can be events like chromothripsis, which is genome fragmentation. It's supposed to be this cataclysmic event for the chromosome where it just shatters into a whole bunch of pieces and gets stuck back together again, like a puzzle except that puzzles usually have ordered way in which they get together but it's just stuck back together. You end up with extrachromosomal DNA and when you have these kinds of events happening, the checking and the replication becomes very error-prone and you end up with a whole huge swathe of mutations that get introduced all at one time. When there's DNA that's outside of the nucleus, this activates the cGAS STING pathway. You're not supposed to have DNA in the cytoplasm, it signals something like an infection, like a virus or DNA in the wrong place. So this has a very strong inflammatory cascade of signaling to it. It quite has a lot of downstream signaling effects and it causes a whole host of stresses for the cell from metabolic stress, proteotoxic stress, replication stress, unfolded protein stress, and ER stress. If this happens in a nonmalignant cell, the cell can handle stress. The cell is used to dealing with it and it has a number ofcell fates that it can employ. The cell will undergo cell cycle arrest, it will die or it will undergo senescence. These are all normal methods that the cell has to deal with these kinds of stresses. However, if it happens in a cancer cell which starts to have these adaptation methods, you end up with a very plastic kind of event and it drives tumor adaptation and adaptability to all these different microenvironments that it might encounter when it starts to metastasize. So you get a lot of things that are protumorigenic when you end up just with this kind of lagging chromosome effect. So yes, there's a lot of cellular consequences for poor mitosis as well.

blocks.label: The Vogelstein multistep model of colorectal cancer progression
blocks.content: Okay. Might want to pick up the pace here. So the Vogelstein model as I said there we were looking again at the progression, the stepwise accumulation of mutations moving from normal to metastatic. So where does chromosomal instability map in this? Well, it maps kind of very early on. It's quite early in looking at this particular model that here you have chromosomal instability or this is FBW7, a mutation in ubiquitin ligase that controls cycling E levels. Right? So this causes genomic instability, this causes defects in replication origin firing and you end up with genomic instability One of the students complained a few years ago, said, "Oh, this image is from 1980 something. Why? [chuckles] It's so old." But the principle of this is exactly the same. It hasn't really changed. The idea that you have mutations that occur very early on. And because, for example, APC mutations appear in adenomas as well as in metastases, we know that these mutations occur early in tumor formation and tumorgenesis. And we also know that mutations in p53 don't appear in things like adenomas, so that we know that this mutation is acquired late in tumor formation. Okay? And here you can see where the oncogenes and the tumor suppressor genes, the mutations are occurring, that help promote the tumor development. So it's not like all the oncogene happen first and all the tumor suppressors mutations happen later. They happen in a dynamic way, and you'll often find many more tumor suppressor genes mutated when you sequence genomes. Right? So for those that don't like 1980s figures, here is 2000 whatever figures. And you'll see that it's exactly the same kind of thing, where there is a mutations that transform the normal epithelium into a hyperplastic epithelium. You've seen this. And then you also get this, as I said, chromosomal instability that starts to drive this process of early, intermediate, and late adenomas moving through acquiring mutations that end up causing frank carcinoma and invasion and metastasis. Okay? But not to portray that there's this linear path in this way. What is clear is that in real tumors, the order of these mutations, as we said, and the number of them, and which ones actually occur is not really known. It varies a lot. So yes, there are a lot of mutations that happen in the APC pathway. Eighty percent of sporadic tumors have this mutation. But then there are question marks as to what is the next mutation that arises and when things happen. The p53 mutations happen quite late, as I said, because they don't show up in the adenomas. So the order of acquisition affects the speed with which the tumors develop. So if you're unlucky enough to get these mutations early, you'll get the tumor that much faster, especially in terms of chromosomal instability. Right? So we don't know which of these mutations happens because there's only indirect evidence that all of these have to be mutated, and that's why there are question marks here.

blocks.label: Two-hit kinetics and population burden of inherited cancer genes
blocks.content: Okay? So, what if you're unlucky enough to be born with a hereditary predisposition to cancer? So, as I said, normally there are two wild type copies we each have. And typically, you'll be unlucky to get a mutation, and then unlucky enough to get another mutation, and this will result in tumor formation. But if you're born with a mutation, it only really takes one other mutation for you to have your cell be abnormal for that function. Right? So in that case, your genetic instability accelerates this process, but if you're born with a slightly abnormal cell to begin with, you're going to be malignant that much quicker.Okay?So it's important to understand this concept because number one, historically, this is how many of the tumor suppressed genes were found, because of the pedigrees of families that had a hereditary predisposition to cancer. And these are also other important genetic diseases. You'll see that breast cancer predisposition is amongst the most lethal uncommon hereditary disease. And you can compare that with other genetic diseases like polycystic kidney disease, one in 500, and cystic fibrosis and spinal muscular atrophy, which are much less common. So it's very common in the population to have a hereditary predisposition to breast cancer. And as you can see, we don't even know all of those genes, because this is one in 300, but only one in 1,000 is a BRCA1 mutation, and only one in 500 is a BRCA2 mutation, so there are more genes to be discovered there.

blocks.label: Clinical features of FAP, Lynch syndrome, hereditary breast cancer, and retinoblastoma
blocks.content: Okay? So just to give you some examples of the hereditary cases that we're talking about, the four of them are listed here. And Lynch syndrome and hereditary predisposition to breast cancer are mutations that affect genetic instability, as we were talking about. Sothese would be known as your caretaker mutations.Right? Mutations that affect the genomic integrity. Whereas APC or FAP, familial adenomatous polyposis, and retinoblastoma are mutations that affect growth control. This is the checkpoint protein, and this is also a protein that's involved in regulating Wnt signaling.Right? So what does that look like? With this adenomatous polyposis coli, this is a mutation that appears early in sporadic cancers.But in people that have this, these individuals inherit this mutation and they end up with a colon that looks something like this, with very large numbers of polyps that develop in the colon over the course of their lives.This is what it might look like in adolescence. Obviously, you can diagnose this with endoscopy, because this is what the normal colon would look like, in terms of smooth and with nice mucin production. But these patients have all of these polyps, and of course, one of them is probably going to progress to adenocarcinoma. So these people rarely survive into adulthood, and so this mutation doesn't really appear that much in the population because they don't reproduce. So it accounts for less than 1% of colorectal cancer cases. Contrast that with Lynch syndrome, which is a mutation in a mismatch repair gene, one of the ones that we were talking about. This results in colon cancer, but without all of those polyps. So if you were to do an endoscopy here, you wouldn't see all of those polyps.[coughing]So this MLH1 mutation occurs in about 15% of sporadic colon cancers. So the genes that are involved in the germline, or the hereditary versions of cancer, are also important in some of the sporadic cancers. But this isn't always the case. Right? So, for example, in hereditary predisposition to breast cancer, BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations are what cause this genetic instability, as we discussed, but these genes are rarely mutated in sporadic breast cancer. They don't really show up So these are about 5% of the breast cancers, and they have a much increased lifetime risk of breast cancer, these individuals. If you compare that to the about 13% risk that other women have in terms of risk of developing breast cancer over your lifetime. So half of those people have a mutation in BRCA1 or BRCA2, and as we said, this is involved in double-strand break repair. Okay? And the last one to talk about is retinoblastoma. This is a mutation in the RB gene. The RB gene goes away, and the cells can progress quite happily through the cell cycle without any need for any upstream regulators or upstream controls. This is a rare childhood tumor. I have written here a half, but it's about a third to a half of retinoblastoma patients have inherited this mutation, and normally it's quite easy to spot this mutation because it shows up in the eye, and you can see it as white lump in the eye. But this mutation, the RB mutation, can occur in both inherited and sporadic cases of the tumor. Right. So I forgot what I wanted to say here [laughs]. Okay.

blocks.label: BRCA2 reversion mutations and malignancy maintenance
blocks.content: Right. But this is the last slide to tell you again, to drive home this point about genetic instability not being required for malignancy. Because if you have a patient that's born with a heterozygous mutation for BRCA2, right, so you have this frame shift. So this is a mutation. Still have a wild type copy, and then somehow, unluckily, this person acquires a second mutation, as we said, over time, and now this person becomes BRCA2 deficient. Right? So now they start to have that unstable genotype, and so they have a tumor, and you start to treat this patient with cisplatin, and this drives tumor evolution, and so the tumor repairs, if you like, via splicing this frameshifted allele. So you go back to having a good or a functional, not perfect, but functional version of BRCA2, and you restore the cancer to being BRCA2 positive. Right? But still, even with this restored function, the cancer still ends up being lethal for the patient because homologous recombination is not really needed for malignancy. Okay? So I hope that covers our learning outcomes for today. I'm happy to answer any questions and happy to recommend some Easter reading as well. This is a good book. It's about 15 years old now, but it takes you all the way through cancer from the 1800s or before to now. Okay? And I'll see you guys on Wednesday when we'll talk through the hallmarks.
